KEY MESSAGE 1...Periods of rain will continue today, then colder air 
will produce scattered wet snow and rain showers tonight through the 
weekend with very minor accumulations possible across higher terrain.

Model guidance has trended a little southeast over the past 24 hours 
with the track of the coastal low, resulting in lower QPF and lower 
snow potential. Any slushy snow accumulations will be meager and 
limited to higher terrain through the weekend with minimal impact.

A highly amplified pattern will develop across CONUS through the end 
of the week, with a sharp ridge over the High Plains and a deep 
downstream trough over the eastern half of the nation. An initial 
surface low over the Ohio Valley this morning will give way to 
secondary coastal cyclogenesis this afternoon just offshore of the 
Delmarva. An elongated coastal low will then move northeast offshore 
of the New England coast tonight through Friday night before 
reaching the Canadian Maritimes Saturday. 

A broad area of frontogenesis and deformation north of the low track 
will cross the eastern Great Lakes today. Light rain will increase 
in coverage early this morning, peaking later this morning before 
starting to taper off from northwest to southeast this afternoon. 
The light rain will mostly end across the Niagara Frontier and Saint 
Lawrence Valley by later this afternoon, while persisting across the 
Southern Tier and Central NY closer to the low track. Rainfall 
amounts have trended down in model guidance, with less than 0.20" in 
most areas. Somewhat higher amounts will fall across the Finger 
Lakes and Central NY, but even here rainfall will likely remain 
below 0.50" today through this evening.

Tonight, the deeper synoptic scale moisture and forcing will 
continue to move east. The broad area of synoptic scale 
precipitation will continue over the far eastern portion of our 
forecast area from the Finger Lakes to southern Tug Hill overnight. 
Some limited lake effect may also develop in Chautauqua County in 
the NNE flow. Otherwise, the rest of the area will be mainly dry for 
much of the night including the Buffalo, Rochester, and Watertown 
areas. 

Cold advection will continue to cool the column and allow for a mix 
with wet snow tonight in areas where precipitation is still falling.
Some wet snow may begin to mix in as early as late afternoon across 
the Tug Hill Plateau, with the change to wet snow then gradually 
progressing to lower elevations overnight. The Tug Hill Plateau and 
western foothills of the Adirondacks may see a slushy inch or so of 
accumulation tonight. A light, slushy coating is also possible 
across the Bristol Hills and Chautauqua Ridge.

Friday through Saturday, cold/moist cyclonic flow will continue over 
the eastern Great Lakes. NNE boundary layer flow Friday morning will 
gradually back to the northwest by Saturday. Synoptic scale moisture 
appears to be lacking on Friday to support any organized lake 
response, with just a few scattered light rain/snow showers 
expected. Latest model guidance suggests and uptick in deep moisture 
Friday night through Saturday night as the main mid level trough 
axis crosses the eastern Great Lakes. This should allow for an 
increase in coverage of lake effect and upslope rain and wet snow 
showers, although the short northerly fetch will still greatly limit 
intensity. Wet snow will be favored for higher terrain, with a 
rain/snow mix for lower elevations closer to the lakeshores.

Spotty light, slushy accumulations are possible across higher 
terrain at times Friday through Saturday night. Total snowfall 
through the period will be meager, with spotty amounts of a coating 
to 2" across the higher terrain of the Tug Hill Plateau, Bristol 
Hills, and Chautauqua Ridge. Little or no accumulation is expected 
for lower elevations.

A few spotty light wet snow and rain showers may continue through 
the first half of Sunday before drier air and subsidence build into 
the eastern Great Lakes, with dry weather returning by evening.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Dry weather will return by early next week, with 
temperatures trending warmer by midweek.

An expansive surface high will build into the Great Lakes and Ohio 
Valley by Monday, bringing a return to dry weather. This high will 
drift very slowly to the east towards the east coast and continue to 
support dry weather for the rest of next week. Temperatures will 
remain cool early in the week, but a strong warming trend will 
develop mid to late week with temperatures rising to well above 
average by Thursday and Friday.
